# PeerVault

> PeerVault sends a file straight from one browser to another with end-to-end encryption, so it never lands on a server you have to pay for or trust.

PeerVault transfers files directly browser-to-browser without server storage. Files are chunked into 64 KB blocks, each encrypted with AES-256-GCM using the Web Crypto API. A lightweight Go relay server handles WebRTC signaling only — it never sees file data. PeerVault is in pre-release and is not published to npm.

## Status

- Pre-release (v1.0.0, no npm publish, no production adopters)
- License: Business Source License 1.1 (BSL 1.1) — not open-source
- Tests: 46 passing (`node --test tests/*.test.mjs`)

## Cryptography — what the code actually implements

Earlier versions of the README and blog claimed "ML-KEM / Kyber hybrid" post-quantum key exchange. **That claim was not accurate and has been retracted.** Inspection of `sdk/src/pq-crypto.ts` reveals:

- `generateECDHKeyPair()` generates a standard P-256 ECDH key pair via WebCrypto.
- `hybridKeyExchange()` calls `crypto.subtle.deriveBits` with `{ name: 'ECDH' }` — classic elliptic-curve DH, not ML-KEM.
- `generateHybridKeyPair()` attempts `crypto.subtle.generateKey({ name: 'ML-KEM-768' })` in a try/catch. Node 24 *does* implement ML-KEM-768 in WebCrypto, but the original call requested the `deriveBits` key usage, which is a Diffie-Hellman operation and is rejected for a KEM — so it always threw and `mlkem` was always `undefined`. Even when the key pair is generated, no encapsulation is performed and its shared secret is never mixed into the HKDF input, so the result is ECDH only either way.
- There is **no lattice arithmetic anywhere in this repository**: no NTT, no polynomial arithmetic mod q=3329, no CBD sampling, no FIPS 203 encapsulation. Verified by search.
- `deriveSharedKey()` correctly applies HKDF-SHA-256 to the ECDH shared secret to derive an AES-256-GCM key.

**In practice the default share-link transfer path does not perform any key exchange at all.** `PeerVaultSender.createShareLink()` calls `CryptoEngine.generateKey()`, which generates a random AES-256-GCM key and base64url-encodes it into the share link's URL fragment; the receiver imports that key directly. Browsers never send the fragment to a server, so the relay cannot decrypt. The ECDH + HKDF code path (`negotiateKey`, `getLocalPublicKey`, `hybridKeyExchange`, `deriveSharedKey`) is exported and functional but is **not called** by `PeerVaultSender` or `PeerVaultReceiver`.

Effective construction: **random AES-256-GCM key in the URL fragment, one fresh 96-bit IV per 64 KB chunk, GCM tag for integrity.** Classical, not post-quantum. The ML-KEM claim must not be repeated to users.

## Real exported symbols

Verified from `sdk/dist/index.mjs`:

- `PeerVaultSender` — manages file selection, WebRTC setup, chunking, encryption, and sending
- `PeerVaultReceiver` — manages joining the room, decrypting chunks, and file assembly
- `PQCrypto` — static class exposing the crypto primitives (ECDH key generation, HKDF derivation, key export/import). `isMLKEMSupported()` is deprecated and returns `false`; use `probeMLKEM()` for a genuine platform feature probe.
- `CryptoEngine` — AES-256-GCM chunk encryption/decryption and key generation/import
- `FileChunker` / `FileAssembler` / `CHUNK_SIZE` — the chunking and reassembly path
- `PeerConnection` / `SignalingClient` / `DEFAULT_ICE_SERVERS` — transport internals, exported so a TURN server can be supplied

## Installation (working paths only)

- jsDelivr CDN: `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/itsoumya-d/peervault@main/sdk/dist/index.mjs`
- Clone and build: `git clone https://github.com/itsoumya-d/peervault && cd peervault/sdk && npm install && npm run build`

## Integration recipe (executed against sdk/dist/index.mjs on Node 24)

```javascript
import { PQCrypto } from 'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/itsoumya-d/peervault@main/sdk/dist/index.mjs';

// Generate ECDH key pair (what the code actually does)
const { publicKey, privateKey } = await PQCrypto.generateECDHKeyPair();

// Export public key for sharing with peer
const exported = await PQCrypto.exportPublicKey(publicKey);
// exported is a base64url string safe to embed in a URL

// Derive shared AES-256-GCM key from ECDH exchange
const peerPublic = await PQCrypto.importPublicKey(exported); // replace with peer's key
const sharedSecret = await PQCrypto.ecdhKeyExchange(privateKey, peerPublic); // hybridKeyExchange() is the same call under an inaccurate name
const aesKey = await PQCrypto.deriveSharedKey(sharedSecret, undefined, 'PeerVault-ECDH-v1');
// aesKey.algorithm.name === 'AES-GCM', aesKey.algorithm.length === 256
```

Full browser-side sender/receiver usage requires a live WebSocket relay server and RTCPeerConnection (browser environment).

## Known limitations

- No TURN relay by default: connections fail behind symmetric or carrier-grade NAT. The default ICE configuration uses three public STUN servers (`stun.l.google.com:19302` x2, `stun.cloudflare.com:3478`) and no TURN server. Pass `{ iceServers: [...] }` to `PeerVaultSender`/`PeerVaultReceiver` to add TURN. A failed ICE negotiation now emits a distinct `error` naming the ICE state, and `connect()` rejects rather than hanging.
- Transfers are not resumable. If either tab closes, the transfer restarts from the beginning.
- The receiver assembles files in memory (`Blob`); measured peak RSS is roughly 1.5x the file size. There is no streaming to disk or IndexedDB.
- Post-quantum cryptography: not implemented. No ML-KEM/Kyber code exists. The effective security is classical.
- File reconstruction is entirely in browser RAM — large files (multi-GB) may exhaust device memory.
- 1:1 only: the relay supports one sender and one receiver per room.
- No npm publication: CDN or git clone only.
